problem: Text-only LLMs given transcribed human audio instructions ignore how things are said (pitch, loudness, duration), so they blindly follow ambiguous or uncertain navigation guidance; existing audio navigation datasets such as RxR do not model vocal uncertainty.
motivation: In social navigation, humans unfamiliar with a place give uncertain guidance, and that uncertainty shows up in vocal delivery as well as wording. Robots need to judge how trustworthy an instruction is and ask for help when it is not. Transcription APIs like Whisper discard the paralinguistic cues that carry this signal.
key_idea: Add prosodic affective cues (pitch, loudness, per-segment duration, aligned to sub-instructions by timestamp) to the Whisper transcript in an in-context CoT prompt, so the LLM can reason about human uncertainty and choose among five next-step actions.
insight: The gain comes from making the vocal cues explicit and letting the LLM reason over them. The transcription-only baseline picks the blind-follow option A for 220 of 500 clips, versus 15 with cues. The ablation shows that without reasoning the cues do not help consistently: the best single cue, loudness, gets 42.31% and all three cues together get 36.93%. With reasoning, all three cues reach 70.46%. The cue-augmented prompt also degrades less under a text-paraphrase attack, because vocal cues survive the text manipulation.
method: Transcription: Whisper-Small with a custom disfluency-eliciting prompt captures hesitations, speech repairs and uncertainty words in the transcript.

Vocal affective cue extraction: an algorithm finds the largest per-second change in loudness and pitch above thresholds, ignoring the first and last 3 s. Sub-instruction durations come from forced alignment, and unusually long segments are flagged. All cues are written as text in the prompt.

In-context CoT choice generation: GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) with 3 few-shot examples (language-only, vocal-only, both) reasons about the unreliable parts and produces 5 options. A is the paraphrased instruction as given, B-D are variants or ask-for-help options, and E is always 'ask another person'.

Choice scoring: the choices and reasoning are passed to GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (also text-davinci-003 and Gemini-1.5-Pro) with logit bias on the tokens A-E. The action is the argmax of the next-token probability, which avoids sequence-length bias.

Confidence metric: C(rho)=1/KL(rho, rho*), comparing the LLM choice distribution with the human-perception distribution. Winning rate is the fraction of clips where the LLM choice matches the human annotation.

DNIA dataset: 500 audio clips from 20 speakers (10 male, 10 female), 10-30 s each, split into 285 language-uncertainty (LU) and 215 vocal-uncertainty (VU, text fluent but voice uncertain) clips. Labels come from a 20-person user study choosing among 5 options.
Adversarial attack: a GPT-4 paraphraser removes uncertainty words and adds certainty words in the transcript, and option A is set to the paraphrase.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen, choice generation) + GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (frozen, scoring); also text-davinci-003 and Gemini-1.5-Pro; Whisper-Small (244M) for transcription
setting.training_data: none (training-free, few-shot in-context prompting with 3 examples)
setting.observation: human speech audio clip, converted to Whisper transcript plus hand-crafted pitch/loudness/duration cues
setting.action_space: 5-way multiple choice over next-step actions (A-E, including ask another person); no low-level control
setting.simulator: none (offline audio dataset DNIA, no simulator)
setting.privileged: none at test time (human-annotated labels used only for evaluation)

numbers.extra: few-shot ICL, uses vocal cues and CoT reasoning
numbers.evidence: Table 'Winning Rate by Context and Audio Type': Ours 70.46% / 72.56% / 68.77% (abstract states 70.26%)

numbers.eval_set_note: all 500 DNIA clips, under adversarial token manipulation attack

numbers_note: Not a standard navigation benchmark. Evaluation is offline winning rate against human labels on the authors' DNIA dataset (labelled 'test' as no official split exists). The abstract says 70.26% while the tables say 70.46%. Baselines: Transcription Only 22.16%, +CoT 49.30%.
results: Beyond Text reaches a 70.46% winning rate on DNIA (72.56% VU, 68.77% LU), against 22.16% for transcription-only GPT-3.5 and 49.30% for the CoT-only baseline. It also helps text-davinci-003 (57.88 to 69.06) and Gemini-1.5-Pro (43.11 to 65.27). Under a token-manipulation attack it drops 33.43% versus 55.87% for text-only.
limitations: Evaluation is offline multiple-choice agreement with human labels on 500 clips from 20 speakers, with no real robot or simulator navigation, so the claim of better navigation is untested.

Cue extraction relies on hand-set thresholds (sensitivity: winning rate falls to about 60-61% at other settings), only uses the single largest pitch/loudness change, and may be biased by accent, gender or distractions.
Uncertainty is ambiguous (self-correction vs. uncertainty), and the approach depends on text transcription and LLM reasoning; the cue ablation is non-monotonic without reasoning.
